title: This New “Devil Flower” Species Doesn’t Photosynthesize - Nautilus
gist: Thismia daemona, a newly identified leafless "devil flower" from Thailand’s Thong Pha Phum National Park, has no chlorophyll and does not photosynthesize, instead drawing nutrients through soil fungi — its horns and eyes being fleshy flower parts called tepals.

insights.claim: The newly identified species Thismia daemona contains no chlorophyll and does not use photosynthesis for nourishment, instead drawing its sustenance through fungi in the soil.
insights.so_what: A species that outsources its core metabolic function to a fungal network is by construction locked to a specific soil biome — extremely habitat-restricted and conservation-fragile.
insights.quote: There’s no chlorophyll in there, and the plant doesn’t use photosynthesis for nourishment.
insights.locator: The tiny horns protruding from the top
insights.speaker: David Nield

insights.claim: Loss of leaves and of chlorophyll are visible diagnostic markers that a plant has switched to fungal dependence, so appearance alone flags the metabolic strategy.
insights.so_what: A cheap field heuristic: pigment and leaf loss signal a parasitic or mycoheterotrophic lifestyle without needing lab work.
insights.quote: their color and the lack of leaves gives something else away
insights.locator: The tiny horns protruding from the top
insights.speaker: David Nield

insights.claim: Thismia daemona was discovered in the forests of Thong Pha Phum National Park in Thailand and resembles a small, charred gremlin with fiery eyes, earning its "devil flower" nickname.
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian protected forests continue to yield undescribed species, which is the empirical case for the conservation value of those specific parks.
insights.locator: Discovered in the forests of the Thong Pha Phum National Park
insights.speaker: David Nield

insights.claim: The apparent horns and glaring eyes of the devil flower are individual fleshy outer parts of the plant known as tepals, not separate structures.
insights.so_what: The striking morphology is an artifact of one floral structure, so the "devil" appearance carries no separate functional story.
insights.quote: The “horns” and “eyes” are actually parts of the flower called tepals.
insights.locator: The “horns” and “eyes” are actually parts of the flower
insights.speaker: David Nield
